source.title: Quantifying Memorization Advantage in Code LLMs
source.authors: Albérick Euraste Djiré; A. K. Kaboré; Jordan Samhi; Earl T. Barr; Jacques Klein; Tegawendé F. Bissyandé

record.tranche_reason: The study measures code LLM sensitivity to input perturbations as a proxy for memorization advantage. It does not test the claim’s train/test generalization gap or any listed version.
record.gate_note: The study reports perturbation-sensitivity outcomes on code tasks. These bear on a related memorization/generalization construct, but not on the behaviors named in V1–V8. Figure distributions are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study measures code LLM performance sensitivity to input paraphrasing and identifier renaming. These results do not test any intervention or comparison in V1–V8. Citing memorization research and interpreting sensitivity as generalization do not establish a test of those versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors interpret task-, benchmark-, and model-dependent sensitivity as evidence about generalization and potential memorization, and recommend perturbation-based evaluation. They acknowledge that unknown training data and limited perturbations prevent definitive attribution. Section 5.1.2 additionally allows that duplication could produce local robustness around memorized examples, explaining low sensitivity on CVEFixes and Defects4J without broader generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Measures code LLM sensitivity to semantically preserving prompt or code perturbations; it does not use the claim’s training interventions or train/test error measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Sensitivity varies by task and benchmark; the study reports higher values for test generation, lower values for code summarization, and distinct patterns on APPS, Defects4J, CVEFixes, and ConDefect.

fits_no_version.finding: Input perturbation sensitivity varies across code models, tasks, and benchmarks: StarCoder has elevated APPS sensitivity, test generation exceeds basic code generation, and Defects4J, CVEFixes, and summarization show relatively low sensitivity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Code LLM robustness to paraphrasing and identifier renaming depends on the model, task, and benchmark; these sensitivity scores alone do not identify memorization or training-data contamination.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE ’26)
record.problems: The authors state that training data are unknown, so they cannot definitively establish leakage or distinguish memorization from generalization. Perturbation methods are limited to paraphrasing and identifier alpha-renaming; different perturbations could yield different patterns. The text reports many distributions only in figures, without recoverable per-model numeric values.
record.rows_left_out: Per-model benchmark distributions in Figures 5–9 are figure-only without textual numeric values, so they were not converted into rows. Other textual benchmark-wide statements without numeric values are represented in the excerpts and not expanded into separate rows.

untested.parts: Fitting fixed random labels, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels under matched architectures and training recipes.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier test error and the roles of local connectivity and initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and changes to training duration or recipe.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness as a predictor of training–test gaps and its ranking against other measures. Input perturbation sensitivity measures a different construct.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and comparing test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; the reported sensitivity differences themselves are supported by the supplied text. The study's statements that memorization can precede generalization do not test random-label coexistence in V1 or example-removal effects in V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Large versus small batch generalization under epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and training/test error gaps.
Removal of memorized examples and resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: StarCoder
rows.operation_detail: Measured perturbation sensitivity on APPS code generation benchmark.
rows.baseline: Other code-generation benchmarks and other models on APPS; exact values not stated.
rows.note: The authors describe this as elevated sensitivity and potential memorization; this is a perturbation proxy, not a train/test error gap.
rows.check: The approximately 0.8 sensitivity and p < 0.01 are supported by Section 4.1, but measure no listed version. The paper inconsistently names the model StarCoder and StarCoder2; its model description and examples indicate StarCoder2 15B.

rows.operation_detail: Measured perturbation sensitivity on Defects4J and other program-repair benchmarks.
rows.note: Aggregate across models. The study interprets lower sensitivity as greater robustness, while acknowledging this does not establish whether data leakage occurred.
rows.check: The sensitivity ranges and significance match Section 4.3. Lower input sensitivity is not a partial effect for any listed version and does not establish absence of leakage.
